claim: Germ cells produce gametes that transmit genetic and epigenetic information to the next generation.
source: The germ line produces gametes that transmit genetic and epigenetic information to the next generation.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about germ cells.

claim: Maintenance of germ cells and development of gametes require germ granules.
source: Maintenance of germ cells and development of gametes require germ granules—well-conserved membraneless and RNA-rich organelles.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Germ granules are well-conserved membraneless and RNA-rich organelles.
source: Maintenance of germ cells and development of gametes require germ granules—well-conserved membraneless and RNA-rich organelles.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about germ granule properties.

claim: The composition of germ granules is elusive owing to their dynamic nature and their exclusive expression in the germ line.
source: The composition of germ granules is elusive owing to their dynamic nature and their exclusive expression in the germ line.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in studying germ granules, based on inference from their properties.

claim: The study employed a proximity-based labeling method in combination with mass spectrometry to comprehensively define P granule protein components.
source: Using Caenorhabditis elegans germ granule, called P granule, as a model system, we employed a proximity-based labeling method in combination with mass spectrometry to comprehensively define its protein components.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The proximity labeling experiments identified over 200 proteins in P granules.
source: This set of experiments identified over 200 proteins, many of which contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many of the identified P granule proteins contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: This set of experiments identified over 200 proteins, many of which contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis of protein sequences using IUPred.

claim: An RNA interference-based screen identified factors that are essential for P granule assembly, notably EGGD-1 and EGGD-2.
source: An RNA interference-based screen identified factors that are essential for P granule assembly, notably EGGD-1 and EGGD-2, two putative LOTUS-domain proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are two putative LOTUS-domain proteins.
source: An RNA interference-based screen identified factors that are essential for P granule assembly, notably EGGD-1 and EGGD-2, two putative LOTUS-domain proteins.
evidence: This is supported by computational domain analysis using HHpred.

claim: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 results in separation of P granules from the nuclear envelope.
source: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 results in separation of P granules from the nuclear envelope, germline atrophy, and reduced fertility.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of mutant animals.

claim: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 results in germline atrophy.
source: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 results in separation of P granules from the nuclear envelope, germline atrophy, and reduced fertility.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations and quantification of germline morphology.

claim: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 results in reduced fertility.
source: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 results in separation of P granules from the nuclear envelope, germline atrophy, and reduced fertility.
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting and germline mortality assays.

claim: IDRs of EGGD-1 are required to anchor EGGD-1 to the nuclear periphery.
source: We show that IDRs of EGGD-1 are required to anchor EGGD-1 to the nuclear periphery while its LOTUS domains are required to promote the perinuclear localization of P granules.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of EGGD-1 domain deletion mutants.

claim: LOTUS domains of EGGD-1 are required to promote the perinuclear localization of P granules.
source: We show that IDRs of EGGD-1 are required to anchor EGGD-1 to the nuclear periphery while its LOTUS domains are required to promote the perinuclear localization of P granules.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of EGGD-1 domain deletion mutants.

claim: Germ granules are known as 'P granules' in worms.
source: For example, they are known as 'P granules' in worms (Strome and Wood, 1982), 'nuage and polar granules' in fruit flies (Mahowald, 1968), 'intermitochondrial cement' in frogs (Bilinski et al., 2004), and 'chromatoid bodies' in mice (Parvinen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Strome and Wood, 1982.

claim: Germ granules are known as 'nuage and polar granules' in fruit flies.
source: For example, they are known as 'P granules' in worms (Strome and Wood, 1982), 'nuage and polar granules' in fruit flies (Mahowald, 1968), 'intermitochondrial cement' in frogs (Bilinski et al., 2004), and 'chromatoid bodies' in mice (Parvinen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mahowald, 1968.

claim: Germ granules are known as 'intermitochondrial cement' in frogs.
source: For example, they are known as 'P granules' in worms (Strome and Wood, 1982), 'nuage and polar granules' in fruit flies (Mahowald, 1968), 'intermitochondrial cement' in frogs (Bilinski et al., 2004), and 'chromatoid bodies' in mice (Parvinen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bilinski et al., 2004.

claim: Germ granules are known as 'chromatoid bodies' in mice.
source: For example, they are known as 'P granules' in worms (Strome and Wood, 1982), 'nuage and polar granules' in fruit flies (Mahowald, 1968), 'intermitochondrial cement' in frogs (Bilinski et al., 2004), and 'chromatoid bodies' in mice (Parvinen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parvinen, 2005.

claim: Common classes of proteins are enriched in germ granules across phyla.
source: Genetic and molecular analyses uncovered common classes of proteins that are enriched in germ granules across phyla (Anderson and Kedersha, 2009; Trcek and Lehmann, 2019; Updike and Strome, 2010; Voronina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: Piwi proteins and their small RNA cofactors—piRNAs—are enriched in germ granules and recognize and silence transposable elements.
source: These include Piwi proteins and their small RNA cofactors—piRNAs that recognize and silence transposable elements Aravin et al., 2006; Brennecke et al., 2007; Lau et al., 2006; Vagin et al., 2006;
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ATP-dependent helicases such as Vasa proteins are enriched in germ granules and are involved in RNA metabolism.
source: ATP-dependent helicases such as Vasa proteins that are involved in RNA metabolism (Gustafson and Wessel, 2010; Spike et al., 2008),
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gustafson and Wessel, 2010 and Spike et al., 2008.

claim: LOTUS-domain proteins are enriched in germ granules.
source: and LOTUS-domain proteins (Limkain /MARF1, Oskar and Tudor domain-containing proteins 5 and 7) (Anantharaman et al., 2010; Callebaut and Mornon, 2010; Kubíková et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Metazoan LOTUS domain proteins promote germ cell development.
source: Metazoan LOTUS domain proteins promote germ cell development.
evidence: This is supported by the examples provided in the following sentences with citations.

claim: Drosophila Oskar interacts with Vasa through its LOTUS domain and serves as scaffold for germ plasm assembly.
source: For example, Drosophila Oskar interacts with Vasa through its LOTUS domain and serves as scaffold for germ plasm assembly (Jeske et al., 2017; Lehmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeske et al., 2017 and Lehmann, 2016.

claim: Mouse TDRD5 and TDRD7 are required for spermatogenesis.
source: Mouse TDRD5 and TDRD7 are required for spermatogenesis (Lachke et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2011; Yabuta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Recent work revealed the identity of three LOTUS-domain proteins in C. elegans.
source: Recent work revealed the identity of three LOTUS-domain proteins in C. elegans and has begun to explore their role in germ granule organization and small RNA biogenesis (Cipriani et al., 2021; Marnik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cipriani et al., 2021 and Marnik et al., 2021.

claim: C. elegans germ granules—P granules—provide an exceptional in vivo model to study granule formation and function.
source: C. elegans germ granules—P granules—provide an exceptional in vivo model to study granule formation and function (Seydoux, 2018; Strome and Wood, 1982; Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: P granules are described as phase‐transitioned condensates.
source: Biophysical studies combined with high-resolution microscopy describe P granules as phase‐transitioned condensates (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brangwynne et al., 2009.

claim: P granules are present in germ cells throughout the entire C. elegans life cycle.
source: P granules are present in germ cells throughout the entire C. elegans life cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P granule biology.

claim: In the adult gonad where germ cells undergo mitosis and differentiation, abundant P granules are associated with the cytoplasmic face of nuclear pores.
source: In the adult gonad where germ cells undergo mitosis and differentiation, abundant P granules are associated with the cytoplasmic face of nuclear pores (Pitt et al., 2000; Sheth et al., 2010; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: During oogenesis, P granules detach from the nuclear membrane and become diffuse in the cytoplasm.
source: During oogenesis, P granules detach from the nuclear membrane and become diffuse in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P granule dynamics.

claim: P granules partition to the posterior of one-cell embryos.
source: Passed on to progeny, P granules partition to the posterior of one-cell embryos.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P granule inheritance.

claim: During cell divisions, P granules are segregated into the germline blastomeres and begin to coalesce and attach to the nuclear periphery.
source: During following cell divisions, P granules are segregated into the germline blastomeres and begin to coalesce and attach to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P granule behavior during development.

claim: P granules ultimately become perinuclear in the primordial germ cells which give rise to the adult germ line.
source: P granules ultimately become perinuclear in the primordial germ cells which give rise to the adult germ line (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: More than 40 protein components are enriched in P granules.
source: More than 40 protein components are enriched in P granules (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: P granule assembly involves core proteins including DEPS-1, GLH-1, PGL-1, and IFE-1.
source: Genetic analyses have revealed an assembly pathway that involves core proteins including DEPS-1, GLH-1, PGL-1, and IFE-1.
evidence: This is supported by established genetic studies.

claim: DEPS-1 is a nematode-specific protein that is required for GLH-1 accumulation.
source: DEPS-1 is a nematode-specific protein that is required for GLH-1 accumulation (Spike et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spike et al., 2008.

claim: GLH-1 belongs to a conserved Vasa family that contributes to germ line development and fertility.
source: GLH-1 belongs to a conserved Vasa family that contributes to germ line development and fertility (Gustafson and Wessel, 2010; Spike et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gustafson and Wessel, 2010 and Spike et al., 2008.

claim: GLH-1 and some of its paralogs contain phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats which are postulated to promote perinuclear localization of P granules.
source: In addition to the conserved DEAD-box helicase domains, GLH-1 and some of its paralogs contain phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats which are postulated to promote perinuclear localization of P granules (Chen et al., 2020; Marnik et al., 2019; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: PGL-1 contains both RNA binding and dimerization domains and serves as a P granule scaffold protein.
source: PGL-1 contains both RNA binding and dimerization domains and serves as a P granule scaffold protein (Aoki et al., 2016; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aoki et al., 2016 and Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claim: Loss of either DEPS-1 or GLH-1 causes dispersal of PGL-1 into the cytoplasm.
source: Loss of either DEPS-1 or GLH-1 causes dispersal of PGL-1 into the cytoplasm, suggesting DEPS-1 and GLH-1 act upstream of PGL-1 (Kawasaki et al., 2004; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kawasaki et al., 2004 and Kawasaki et al., 1998.

claim: DEPS-1 and GLH-1 act upstream of PGL-1.
source: Loss of either DEPS-1 or GLH-1 causes dispersal of PGL-1 into the cytoplasm, suggesting DEPS-1 and GLH-1 act upstream of PGL-1 (Kawasaki et al., 2004; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis data cited.

claim: IFE-1 is a C. elegans homolog of eIF4E, an mRNA cap-binding protein.
source: IFE-1 is a C. elegans homolog of eIF4E, an mRNA cap-binding protein (Keiper et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keiper et al., 2000.

claim: IFE-1 and PGL-1 interact directly.
source: IFE-1 and PGL-1 interact directly and the association of IFE-1 with P granules depends on PGL-1 (Amiri et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amiri et al., 2001.

claim: The association of IFE-1 with P granules depends on PGL-1.
source: IFE-1 and PGL-1 interact directly and the association of IFE-1 with P granules depends on PGL-1 (Amiri et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amiri et al., 2001.

claim: P granule components are primarily identified by genetic approaches.
source: So far, P granule components are primarily identified by genetic approaches (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: P granules cannot be easily purified via a conventional fractionation-based approach due to their perinuclear localization and the nature of membraneless compartments.
source: Due to their perinuclear localization and the nature of membraneless compartments, P granules cannot be easily purified via a conventional fractionation-based approach.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical properties of P granules.

claim: TurboID is an engineered promiscuous biotin ligase derived from bacterial BirA that generates reactive biotin derivatives that label proteins in close proximity to the enzyme.
source: TurboID—an engineered promiscuous biotin ligase derived from bacterial BirA—generates reactive biotin derivatives that label proteins in close proximity to the enzyme (Branon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Branon et al., 2018.

claim: TurboID is active from 20°C to 25°C, a range of temperature suitable for C. elegans cultivation.
source: TurboID is active from 20°C to 25°C, a range of temperature suitable for C. elegans cultivation (Branon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Branon et al., 2018.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 was used to introduce TurboID sequences to genomic loci of deps-1, glh-1, pgl-1, or ife-1.
source: To this end, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to introduce TurboID sequences to genomic loci of deps-1, glh-1, pgl-1, or ife-1, which encode proteins known to reside in P granules (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used, as shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Strains expressing DEPS-1::TurboID produced ~88 progeny/animal.
source: We found that strains expressing DEPS-1::TurboID and TurboID::GLH-1 yielded ~88 and ~167 progeny/animal, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Strains expressing TurboID::GLH-1 produced ~167 progeny/animal.
source: We found that strains expressing DEPS-1::TurboID and TurboID::GLH-1 yielded ~88 and ~167 progeny/animal, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TurboID::ife-1 animals on average produced ~77 progeny.
source: The brood size of TurboID::ife-1 animals exhibited a large variation. A small portion of animals became completely sterile and each animal on average produced ~77 progeny (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The strain expressing PGL-1::TurboID was completely sterile.
source: The strain expressing PGL-1::TurboID was completely sterile, a phenotype that is more severe than pgl-1 null mutants (Figure 1B; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sterility phenotype of PGL-1::TurboID is more severe than pgl-1 null mutants.
source: The strain expressing PGL-1::TurboID was completely sterile, a phenotype that is more severe than pgl-1 null mutants (Figure 1B; Kawasaki et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published data on pgl-1 null mutants.

claim: The expression of TurboID could cause toxicity.
source: This finding suggests that the expression of TurboID could cause toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the severe sterility phenotype of PGL-1::TurboID.

claim: PGL-1::TagRFP is primarily perinuclear in deps-1::TurboID and TurboID::glh-1 strains.
source: Similar to wild-type animals, PGL-1::TagRFP and GFP::CSR-1 are primarily perinuclear in both TurboID animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP::CSR-1 is primarily perinuclear in deps-1::TurboID and TurboID::glh-1 strains.
source: Similar to wild-type animals, PGL-1::TagRFP and GFP::CSR-1 are primarily perinuclear in both TurboID animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: More proteins were biotinylated in strains expressing DEPS-1::TurboID and TurboID::GLH-1 compared to untagged control.
source: In strains expressing DEPS-1::TurboID and TurboID::GLH-1, more proteins were biotinylated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by streptavidin-HRP blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Signals of biotinylated proteins were observed in the cytoplasm, but highly enriched in perinuclear structures in deps-1::TurboID and TurboID::glh-1 gonads.
source: In the deps-1::TurboID and TurboID::glh-1 gonads, signals of biotinylated proteins were observed in the cytoplasm, but highly enriched in perinuclear structures (Figure 1D, middle and bottom panels).
evidence: This is supported by streptavidin staining images shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TurboID can be applied to label proteins in C. elegans germ line.
source: These findings indicate that TurboID can be applied to label proteins in C. elegans germ line.
evidence: This is inferred from the biotinylation assay results.

claim: 155 proteins were significantly enriched by labeling with TurboID::GLH-1 compared to untagged control.
source: As compared to untagged control, 155 and 127 proteins were significantly enriched by labeling with TurboID::GLH-1 and DEPS-1::TurboID, respectively (fold change ≥8, p<0.05) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 127 proteins were significantly enriched by labeling with DEPS-1::TurboID compared to untagged control.
source: As compared to untagged control, 155 and 127 proteins were significantly enriched by labeling with TurboID::GLH-1 and DEPS-1::TurboID, respectively (fold change ≥8, p<0.05) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 38.2% (78/204) of the combined 204 candidates were recovered from both deps-1::TurboID and TurboID::glh-1 strains.
source: Of the combined 204 candidates, 38.2% (78/204) were recovered from both deps-1::TurboID and TurboID::glh-1 strains (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the Venn diagram shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The streptavidin affinity enrichment recovered 90% (18/20) of known P granule proteins.
source: Our streptavidin affinity enrichment recovered 90% (18/20) of known P granule proteins and all Z granule proteins—ZNFX-1 and WAGO-4 (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with known P granule proteins listed in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The streptavidin affinity enrichment recovered all Z granule proteins—ZNFX-1 and WAGO-4.
source: Our streptavidin affinity enrichment recovered 90% (18/20) of known P granule proteins and all Z granule proteins—ZNFX-1 and WAGO-4 (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with known Z granule proteins.

claim: None of the proteins (0/11) in Mutator foci were enriched.
source: In contrast, none of the proteins (0/11) in Mutator foci were enriched (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with known Mutator foci proteins.

claim: P granules physically contact Z granules, but not Mutator foci.
source: Our result is consistent with the previous finding that P granules physically contact Z granules, but not Mutator foci (Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wan et al., 2018 and is consistent with the TurboID enrichment data.

claim: The PGL family members PGL-1 and PGL-3 were enriched in both TurboID experiments.
source: For example, the PGL family members PGL-1 and PGL-3, and four Vasa family members GLH-1, GLH-2, GLH-3, and GLH-4 were enriched (Gruidl et al., 1996; Kawasaki et al., 2004; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Spike et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Four Vasa family members GLH-1, GLH-2, GLH-3, and GLH-4 were enriched in both TurboID experiments.
source: For example, the PGL family members PGL-1 and PGL-3, and four Vasa family members GLH-1, GLH-2, GLH-3, and GLH-4 were enriched (Gruidl et al., 1996; Kawasaki et al., 2004; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Spike et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: WAGO-1, WAGO-4, CSR-1, and PRG-1 are Argonaute proteins localized to P granules.
source: These include WAGO-1, WAGO-4, CSR-1, and PRG-1 localized to P granules as well as PPW-1/WAGO-7 and PPW-2/WAGO-3 whose localization requires further investigation (Batista et al., 2008; Claycomb et al., 2009; Das et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2018; Yigit et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: PPW-1/WAGO-7 and PPW-2/WAGO-3 localization requires further investigation.
source: These include WAGO-1, WAGO-4, CSR-1, and PRG-1 localized to P granules as well as PPW-1/WAGO-7 and PPW-2/WAGO-3 whose localization requires further investigation (Batista et al., 2008; Claycomb et al., 2009; Das et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2018; Yigit et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the need for further research.

claim: HRDE-1/WAGO-9, a germline nuclear Argonaute protein, was not enriched.
source: Of note, HRDE-1/WAGO-9, a germline nuclear Argonaute protein was not enriched, suggesting TurboID preferentially labeled P granule proteins (Buckley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: TurboID preferentially labeled P granule proteins.
source: Of note, HRDE-1/WAGO-9, a germline nuclear Argonaute protein was not enriched, suggesting TurboID preferentially labeled P granule proteins (Buckley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of nuclear Argonaute protein HRDE-1 in the enrichment.

claim: Many factors involved in RNA synthesis, processing, and decay were enriched.
source: Consistent with the idea that germ granules are hubs for RNA metabolism (Trcek and Lehmann, 2019), many factors involved in RNA synthesis, processing, and decay were enriched.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data and is consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Components of cytoplasmic filaments NPP-9 and NPP-14, and cytoplasmic ring component NPP-6 were significantly enriched in both TurboID experiments.
source: Indeed, components of cytoplasmic filaments NPP-9 and NPP-14, and cytoplasmic ring component NPP-6 were significantly enriched in both TurboID experiments (Figure 2B and C, Supplementary file 3; Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: TurboID proximity labeling can be applied to enrich proteins within P granules.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that TurboID proximity labeling can be applied to enrich proteins within P granules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The top three enriched GO terms in the domain of cellular component were 'cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein granule,' 'ribonucleoprotein granule,' and 'P granule'.
source: As expected, the top three enriched GO terms in the domain of cellular component were 'cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein granule,' 'ribonucleoprotein granule,' and 'P granule' (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the domain of biological process, the top GO terms are 'negative regulation of gene expression,' 'gene silencing by RNA,' and 'posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression'.
source: In the domain of biological process, the top GO terms are 'negative regulation of gene expression,' 'gene silencing by RNA,' and 'posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression' (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GO terms including 'oocyte construction' and 'oocyte anterior/posterior axis specification' were highly enriched.
source: Additionally, GO terms including 'oocyte construction' and 'oocyte anterior/posterior axis specification' were highly enriched (Supplementary file 4), consistent with the notion that P granules are essential for gametogenesis and germ line maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: In the domain of molecular function, GO terms including 'RNA binding,' 'nucleic acid binding' and 'helicase activity' were significantly enriched.
source: In the domain of molecular function, GO terms including 'RNA binding,' 'nucleic acid binding' and 'helicase activity' were significantly enriched, suggesting P granule proteins interact extensively with RNAs (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: P granule proteins interact extensively with RNAs.
source: In the domain of molecular function, GO terms including 'RNA binding,' 'nucleic acid binding' and 'helicase activity' were significantly enriched, suggesting P granule proteins interact extensively with RNAs (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of RNA-related GO terms.

claim: The P granule protein interaction network contained 78 nodes and 200 non-redundant edges.
source: When examining proteins labeled by both DEPS-1::TurboID and TurboID::GLH-1, we found the resulting network contained 78 nodes and 200 non-redundant edges (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by STRING network analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of edges in the P granule protein interaction network was significantly higher than expected by chance (p<1 ×10–16).
source: The number of edges was significantly higher than expected by chance (p<1 ×10–16), implying that the proteins are at least partially biologically connected as a group and multiple PPIs may act in P granule assembly.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the protein interaction network.

claim: The proteins are at least partially biologically connected as a group and multiple PPIs may act in P granule assembly.
source: The number of edges was significantly higher than expected by chance (p<1 ×10–16), implying that the proteins are at least partially biologically connected as a group and multiple PPIs may act in P granule assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the network analysis results.

claim: Compared to a randomly selected control group, the P granule proteome displayed a higher degree of disorder.
source: Compared to a randomly selected control group the P granule proteome displayed a higher degree of disorder (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by IUPred analysis shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: IDR-containing proteins are overrepresented in P granules.
source: These data suggest that IDR-containing proteins are overrepresented in P granules.
evidence: This is inferred from the disorder analysis results.

claim: Out of 31 genes screened, 11 genes upon depletion caused PGL-1::TagRFP phenotypes in adult animals.
source: Out of 31 genes, we screened so far 11 genes upon depletion caused PGL-1::TagRFP phenotypes in adult animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screening results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Depletion of cpf-2 has been reported to be required for proper PGL-1 localization.
source: Among these 11 genes, cpf-2 has been reported to be required for proper PGL-1 localization (Updike and Strome, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2009.

claim: Depletion of cey-2 and cey-3 induces PGL-1 aggregation.
source: A recent study showed that depletion of cey-2 and cey-3, two genes encoding Y-box binding proteins, induces PGL-1 aggregation (Calculli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calculli et al., 2021.

claim: Depletion of C38D4.4 resulted in the formation of large PGL-1-containing aggregates, many of which are separated from the nuclear envelope of germ cells.
source: Depletion of C38D4.4 resulted in the formation of large PGL-1-containing aggregates, many of which are separated from the nuclear envelope of germ cells.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C38D4.4 was named eggd-1 for embryonic and germline P granule detached.
source: Based on this phenotype, we named C38D4.4 as eggd-1 for embryonic and germline P granule detached.
evidence: This is a naming decision based on the observed phenotype.

claim: F58G11.3 is a predicted paralog of EGGD-1.
source: F58G11.3 is a predicted paralog of EGGD-1.
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis.

claim: F58G11.3 is 33.3% identical to EGGD-1 at the amino acid level.
source: It is 33.3% identical to EGGD-1 at the amino acid level.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: F58G11.3 was identified from TurboID experiments.
source: Interestingly, F58G11.3 was also identified from TurboID experiments (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: F58G11.3 was named eggd-2.
source: We named F58G11.3 as eggd-2, although RNAi against F58G11.3 did not yield noticeable change in PGL-1::TagRFP localization (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a naming decision.

claim: RNAi against F58G11.3 did not yield noticeable change in PGL-1::TagRFP localization.
source: We named F58G11.3 as eggd-2, although RNAi against F58G11.3 did not yield noticeable change in PGL-1::TagRFP localization (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screening results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An independent study refers to EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 as MEG-3 interacting proteins MIP-1 and MIP-2, respectively.
source: Of note, an independent study refers to EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 as MEG-3 interacting proteins MIP-1 and MIP-2, respectively (Cipriani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cipriani et al., 2021.

claim: PGL-1::TagRFP was dispersed into the cytoplasm in eggd-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with the result from RNAi experiments, PGL-1::TagRFP was dispersed into the cytoplasm in eggd-1 mutants (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Neither of eggd-2 alleles yielded noticeable change in PGL-1::TagRFP localization in the pachytene region.
source: Neither of eggd-2 alleles yielded noticeable change in PGL-1::TagRFP localization in the pachytene region (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In eggd-1 mutants, fewer PGL-1 foci were perinuclear, and most diffused into the rachis.
source: In eggd-1 mutants, however, fewer PGL-1 foci were perinuclear, and most diffused into the rachis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Loss of eggd-2 appeared to have a minor effect on PGL-1 localization.
source: Loss of eggd-2 appeared to have a minor effect on PGL-1 localization (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deletion of both eggd-1 and eggd-2 caused dispersal of perinuclear PGL-1::TagRFP and accumulation of large cytoplasmic PGL-1 aggregates.
source: Deletion of both eggd-1 and eggd-2 caused dispersal of perinuclear PGL-1::TagRFP and accumulation of large cytoplasmic PGL-1 aggregates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rachis/edge ratio was increased in eggd-1 mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Compared to that in wild-type, the rachis/edge ratio was increased in eggd-1 mutants, and further increased in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of PGL-1::TagRFP signal shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The rachis/edge ratio was further increased in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants compared to eggd-1 single mutants.
source: Compared to that in wild-type, the rachis/edge ratio was increased in eggd-1 mutants, and further increased in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of PGL-1::TagRFP signal shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PGL-1 failed to concentrate in the germ lineage in eggd-1, eggd-2, and eggd-1; eggd-2 embryos.
source: In contrast, PGL-1 failed to concentrate in the germ lineage in eggd-1, eggd-2, and eggd-1; eggd-2 embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Perinuclear P granules were not formed in comma stage embryos upon loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2.
source: Furthermore, perinuclear P granules were not formed in comma stage embryos upon loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 promote the perinuclear localization of P granules in both adult germ lines and embryos.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 promote the perinuclear localization of P granules in both adult germ lines and embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypes observed in mutants.

claim: Both eggd-1 and eggd-2 mutants displayed a diminutive germ line compared to wild-type animals.
source: Both eggd-1 and eggd-2 mutants displayed a diminutive germ line compared to wild-type animals (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Additive genetic effects were observed in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants for germ line size.
source: Additive genetic effects were observed in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The wild-type strain produced ~263 progeny/animal.
source: The wild-type strain produced ~263 progeny/animal (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: eggd-1 animals produced ~170 progeny/animal.
source: As compared to wild-type, eggd-1 and eggd-2 animals displayed moderate reduction in brood size, generating ~170 and ~204 progeny/animal, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: eggd-2 animals produced ~204 progeny/animal.
source: As compared to wild-type, eggd-1 and eggd-2 animals displayed moderate reduction in brood size, generating ~170 and ~204 progeny/animal, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants produced only ~37 progeny/animal.
source: Strikingly, eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants exhibited an additive fertility deficit and produced only ~37 progeny/animal (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants exhibited an additive fertility deficit.
source: Strikingly, eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants exhibited an additive fertility deficit and produced only ~37 progeny/animal (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by brood size counting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Animals deficient for EGGD-1 or EGGD-2 exhibited decline in fertility over generations.
source: Animals deficient for EGGD-1 or EGGD-2 exhibited decline in fertility over generations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the mortal germ line assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants became sterile more rapidly when compared to single mutants.
source: The eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants became sterile more rapidly when compared to single mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the mortal germ line assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are required for the maintenance and immortality of C. elegans germ line.
source: Altogether, these observations suggest that EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are required for the maintenance and immortality of C. elegans germ line.
evidence: This is inferred from the fertility and germ line mortality data.

claim: Both EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 were relatively disordered.
source: First, both EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 were relatively disordered (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by IUPred analysis.

claim: Two IDRs were identified in EGDD-1 and EGGD-2, one close to their N-termini and the other located at their C-termini.
source: Based on IUPred algorithm, two IDRs were identified in EGDD-1 and EGGD-2, one close to their N-termini and the other located at their C-termini (Figure 4A and B; Dosztányi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by IUPred analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Both EGGD-1::GFP and mCherry::EGGD-2 are expressed in the adult germ line and germ lineage of embryos.
source: Both proteins are expressed in the adult germ line and germ lineage of embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Both EGGD-1::GFP and mCherry::EGGD-2 localize to perinuclear P granules.
source: Consistent with the TurboID data, both EGGD-1::GFP and mCherry::EGGD-2 localize to perinuclear P granules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The fluorescent signal of EGGD-2 was much weaker than EGGD-1::GFP or PGL-1::TagRFP.
source: Of note, the fluorescent signal of EGGD-2 was much weaker than EGGD-1::GFP or PGL-1::TagRFP.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: Full-length EGGD-1::GFP partly co-localized with PGL-1::TagRFP foci.
source: In the adult germ line, full-length EGGD-1::GFP partly co-localized with PGL-1::TagRFP foci (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: EGGD-1::GFP foci surround PGL-1::TagRFP foci in some instances, but largely are enriched at the base of P granules.
source: Super-resolution imaging revealed that EGGD-1::GFP foci surround PGL-1::TagRFP foci in some instances, but largely are enriched at the base of P granules (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: When the first LOTUS domain was deleted (ΔLOTUS 1), EGGD-1 displayed prominent perinuclear localization while PGL-1::tagRFP was mislocalized.
source: When the first LOTUS domain was deleted (ΔLOTUS 1), EGGD-1 displayed prominent perinuclear localization. In contrast, PGL-1::tagRFP was mislocalized.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon removal of the second LOTUS domain (ΔLOTUS 2), EGGD-1 localized to the nuclear periphery while perinuclear PGL-1 foci were modestly lost.
source: Upon removal of the second LOTUS domain (ΔLOTUS 2), EGGD-1 localized to the nuclear periphery while perinuclear PGL-1 foci were modestly lost.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of both LOTUS one and LOTUS two did not appear to affect EGGD-1 localization, but PGL-1 became predominantly cytoplasmic.
source: Deletion of both LOTUS one and LOTUS two did not appear to affect EGGD-1 localization. However, PGL-1 became predominantly cytoplasmic (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the first IDR was deleted (ΔIDR 1), perinuclear EGGD-1 foci remained, but some EGGD-1 became dispersed into the cytoplasm.
source: When the first IDR was deleted (ΔIDR 1), perinuclear EGGD-1 foci remained, but some EGGD-1 became dispersed into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the second IDR was deleted (ΔIDR 2), both EGGD-1 and PGL-1::tagRFP foci were largely attached to the nuclear periphery albeit the presence of some large aggregates.
source: When the second IDR was deleted (ΔIDR 2), both EGGD-1 and PGL-1::tagRFP foci were largely attached to the nuclear periphery albeit the presence of some large aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When both IDR one and IDR two were deleted, EGGD-1 was almost completely dispersed in the cytoplasm in the pachytene region and PGL-1::TagRFP became cytoplasmic.
source: When both IDR one and IDR two were deleted, we found that EGGD-1 was almost completely dispersed in the cytoplasm in the pachytene region. And similarly, PGL-1::TagRFP became cytoplasmic (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: LOTUS domains and IDRs in EGGD-1 have distinct roles in promoting perinuclear P granules: IDRs are required to anchor EGGD-1 protein to the nuclear periphery, and LOTUS domains likely recruit additional P granule proteins.
source: These findings imply that LOTUS domains and IDRs in EGGD-1 have distinct roles in promoting perinuclear P granules: IDRs are required to anchor EGGD-1 protein to the nuclear periphery, and LOTUS domains likely recruit additional P granule proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the domain deletion experiments.

claim: When eggd-1 was deleted, GFP::GLH-1 became diffuse and most of the protein was no longer associated with the nuclear periphery.
source: However, when eggd-1 was deleted, GFP::GLH-1 became diffuse and most of the protein was no longer associated with the nuclear periphery (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of eggd-2 did not appear to affect GFP::GLH-1 localization.
source: Deletion of eggd-2 did not appear to affect GFP::GLH-1 localization.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a striking change in GFP:GLH-1 distribution in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutant animals, with the majority of fluorescence signals appearing throughout the cytoplasm.
source: There was a striking change in GFP:GLH-1 distribution in eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutant animals, with the majority of fluorescence signals appearing throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Perinuclear GFP::GLH-1 primarily depends on EGGD-1.
source: These findings suggest perinuclear GFP::GLH-1 primarily depends on EGGD-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis results.

claim: PGL-1::TagRFP became diffused into the cytoplasm upon depletion of GLH protein(s).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Spike et al., 2008), PGL-1::TagRFP became diffused into the cytoplasm upon depletion of GLH protein(s).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EGGD-1::GFP remained at the nuclear periphery upon depletion of GLH protein(s).
source: In contrast, EGGD-1::GFP remained at the nuclear periphery (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Perinuclear localization of EGGD-1 does not rely on the GLH family.
source: These observations suggest that unlike other P granule proteins, perinuclear localization of EGGD-1 does not rely on the GLH family.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Depletion of npp-10 caused diffuse PGL-1::TagRFP.
source: Indeed, depletion of npp-10 caused diffuse PGL-1::TagRFP (Updike and Strome, 2009; Voronina and Seydoux, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments and citations.

claim: EGGD-1::GFP became detached from the nuclear membrane and formed aggregates in the cytoplasm upon depletion of npp-10.
source: Similarly, EGGD-1::GFP became detached from the nuclear membrane and formed aggregates in the cytoplasm upon depletion of npp-10 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Perinuclear EGGD-1 requires intact nuclear pores.
source: Taken together, the epistasis analysis demonstrates perinuclear EGGD-1 requires intact nuclear pores and recruitment of GLH-1 to the nuclear periphery depends on EGGD-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis results.

claim: Recruitment of GLH-1 to the nuclear periphery depends on EGGD-1.
source: Taken together, the epistasis analysis demonstrates perinuclear EGGD-1 requires intact nuclear pores and recruitment of GLH-1 to the nuclear periphery depends on EGGD-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis results.

claim: mCherry::GLH-1 was diffuse throughout the cytoplasm in muscle cells.
source: Consistent with previous findings that wild-type GLH-1 cannot form granules by itself (Updike et al., 2011), mCherry::GLH-1 was diffuse throughout the cytoplasm in muscle cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EGGD-1::GFP self-aggregated into granules when it was expressed ectopically.
source: In contrast, EGGD-1::GFP self-aggregated into granules when it was expressed ectopically.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The majority of EGGD-1::GFP granules appeared to associate with the nuclear periphery when expressed ectopically.
source: While a few cytoplasmic granules were observed, the majority of EGGD-1::GFP granules appeared to associate with the nuclear periphery (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When EGGD-1::GFP and mCherry::GLH-1 were expressed simultaneously, both proteins co-localized and formed perinuclear foci.
source: Strikingly, both proteins co-localized and formed perinuclear foci (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: EGGD-1 is intrinsically capable of forming perinuclear granules.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that EGGD-1 is intrinsically capable of forming perinuclear granules, and drives the formation of perinuclear granules by recruiting GLH-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the ectopic expression experiments.

claim: EGGD-1 drives the formation of perinuclear granules by recruiting GLH-1.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that EGGD-1 is intrinsically capable of forming perinuclear granules, and drives the formation of perinuclear granules by recruiting GLH-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the ectopic expression experiments.

claim: P granule formation requires core components including PGL family members PGL-1 and PGL-3, and Vasa family members GLH-1 and GLH-4.
source: Previous studies showed that P granule formation requires core components including PGL family members PGL-1 and PGL-3, and Vasa family members GLH-1 and GLH-4 (Gruidl et al., 1996; Kawasaki et al., 2004; Kawasaki et al., 1998; Spike et al., 2008; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Zygotic P granule assembly requires intrinsically disordered proteins MEG-3 and MEG-4.
source: Zygotic P granule assembly further requires intrinsically disordered proteins MEG-3 and MEG-4 (Smith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Both studies reveal that LOTUS-domain proteins are required for C. elegans germline development and fertility.
source: Both studies reveal that LOTUS-domain proteins are required for C. elegans germline development and fertility.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from this study and Cipriani et al., 2021.

claim: Cipriani et al show that MIPs physically interact with GLH-1 using in vitro pull-down and yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Using in vitro pull-down and yeast two-hybrid assays, Cipriani et al show that MIPs physically interact with GLH-1, a member of the Vasa family (Cipriani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cipriani et al., 2021.

claim: IDRs of EGGD proteins may form multivalent interactions with cytoplasmic filaments of the nuclear pore complex.
source: IDRs of EGGD proteins may form multivalent interactions with cytoplasmic filaments of the nuclear pore complex.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: IDRs preferentially associate with phenylalanine/glycine-rich NPPs that are intrinsically disordered.
source: It is possible that IDRs preferentially associate with phenylalanine/glycine-rich NPPs that are intrinsically disordered (Marnik et al., 2019; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the properties of IDRs and NPPs.

claim: Dimerization of LOTUS domains may serve as an interface for the binding of Vasa protein GLH-1.
source: Dimerization of LOTUS domains may serve as an interface for the binding of Vasa protein GLH-1 (Cipriani et al., 2021; Jeske et al., 2015; Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on known properties of LOTUS domains and citations.

claim: Association of GLH-1 with the nuclear periphery initiates the recruitment of PGL-1 and additional P granule proteins.
source: Association of GLH-1 with the nuclear periphery initiates the recruitment of PGL-1 and additional P granule proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: In the adult germ line, EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 function partially redundantly.
source: In the adult germ line, EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 function partially redundantly.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypes of single and double mutants.

claim: EGGD-1 plays a more dominant role in promoting the perinuclear localization of P granules in the adult germ line.
source: EGGD-1 plays a more dominant role in promoting the perinuclear localization of P granules (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypes shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the embryos, both EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are required for P granule partitioning and attachment to the nuclear periphery.
source: In the embryos, however, both proteins are required for P granule partitioning and attachment to the nuclear periphery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 may interact with different Vasa proteins and thus make distinct contributions to P granule assembly in the germ line and zygotes.
source: One speculative explanation is that EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 interact with different Vasa proteins and thus make distinct contributions to P granule assembly in the germ line and zygotes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the differential roles of EGGD-1 and EGGD-2.

claim: Most LOTUS domain proteins, including Oskar, TDRD5, and TDRD7, harbor a single eLOTUS domain.
source: Most LOTUS domain proteins, including Oskar, TDRD5, and TDRD7, harbor a single eLOTUS domain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about LOTUS domain proteins.

claim: EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are predicted to contain two eLOTUS domains.
source: In contrast, EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are predicted to contain two eLOTUS domains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by computational domain analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The eLOTUS domain of Drosophilla Oskar is capable of forming dimers.
source: The eLOTUS domain of Drosophilla Oskar is capable of forming dimers (Jeske et al., 2015; Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeske et al., 2015 and Jeske et al., 2017.

claim: Recombinant MIP-1 physically interacts with itself and MIP-2 in vitro.
source: In vitro pull-down assays revealed that recombinant MIP-1 physically interacts with itself and MIP-2 (Cipriani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cipriani et al., 2021.

claim: EGGD-1 self-aggregates into granules when expressed ectopically.
source: Here we show EGGD-1 self-aggregates into granules when expressed ectopically (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6.

claim: MIP-1/EGGD-1 and MIP-2/EGGD-2 may form homodimers, heterodimers, or even oligomers in vivo through their eLOTUS domains.
source: It is possible that MIP-1/EGGD-1 and MIP-2/EGGD-2 form homodimers, heterodimers, or even oligomers in vivo through their eLOTUS domains.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the properties of eLOTUS domains.

claim: An independent study identified a third LOTUS domain protein LOTR-1 which is homologous to mammalian TDRD5/7.
source: Of note, an independent study identified a third LOTUS domain protein LOTR-1 which is homologous to mammalian TDRD5/7 (Marnik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marnik et al., 2021.

claim: LOTR-1 was enriched from TurboID experiments.
source: Interestingly, similar to EGGD-1 and EGGD-2, LOTR-1 was also enriched from our TurboID experiments (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LOTUS domains exhibit minimum sequence homology.
source: LOTUS domains exhibit minimum sequence homology (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Anantharaman et al., 2010; Callebaut and Mornon, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: LOTUS domains adopt a common helix-turn-helix conformation.
source: Yet they adopt a common helix-turn-helix conformation (Anantharaman et al., 2010; Callebaut and Mornon, 2010; Jeske et al., 2015; Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The fact that diverse sequences yield a similar structure implies that the LOTUS domain acts as a structural scaffold.
source: The fact that diverse sequences yield a similar structure implies that the LOTUS domain acts as a structural scaffold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural properties of LOTUS domains.

claim: The conserved function of eLOTUS domains is to bind to Vasa.
source: Indeed, the conserved function of eLOTUS domains is to bind to Vasa (Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeske et al., 2017.

claim: LOTUS proteins are essential for the development of metazoan germ cells.
source: Consistent with the idea the structure of a protein largely determines its functional properties, LOTUS proteins are essential for the development of metazoan germ cells.
evidence: This is supported by the examples provided in the following sentences with citations.

claim: In Drosophila, Oskar is required for germ plasm assembly and germ cell formation.
source: In Drosophila, Oskar is required for germ plasm assembly and germ cell formation (Jeske et al., 2017; Lehmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeske et al., 2017 and Lehmann, 2016.

claim: In mice, TDRD7 localizes to chromatoid bodies and is required for spermatogenesis.
source: In mice, TDRD7 localizes to chromatoid bodies (P granule counterpart), and is required for spermatogenesis (Lachke et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2004; Tanaka et al., 2011; Yabuta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: C. elegans EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are key components for germ granule assembly on the nuclear periphery.
source: In this study, we show that C. elegans EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are key components for germ granule assembly on the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: LOTUS domain proteins belong to a unique family that has low sequence identity, but high structure homology and functional similarity.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that LOTUS domain proteins belong to a unique family that has low sequence identity, but high structure homology and functional similarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of LOTUS domain proteins across species.

claim: Proximity labeling is a powerful approach to map the proteome composition of organelles in living cells.
source: Proximity labeling is a powerful approach to map the proteome composition of organelles in living cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about proximity labeling methods.

claim: The key advantage of proximity labeling lies in its ability to capture weak and transient interaction.
source: Compared to conventional affinity purification, the key advantage lies in its ability to capture weak and transient interaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the advantages of proximity labeling.

claim: The strong binding of biotin to streptavidin permits stringent protein extraction which reduces background contaminants.
source: In addition, the strong binding of biotin to streptavidin permits stringent protein extraction which reduces background contaminants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about biotin-streptavidin interaction.

claim: Proximity labeling is an ideal tool to define the composition of phase-separated membraneless organelles that are formed by weak multivalent interactions.
source: It is therefore an ideal tool to define the composition of phase-separated membraneless organelles that are formed by weak multivalent interactions (Bracha et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of proximity labeling and membraneless organelles.

claim: TurboID appears to be the best choice for C. elegans labeling.
source: TurboID appears to be the best choice for C. elegans labeling for several reasons:
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of TurboID.

claim: TurboID uses ATP and biotin as substrates which are readily available in cells, while APEX requires exogenous cofactors which may not be easily transported into worms.
source: (2) TurboID uses ATP and biotin as substrates which are readily available in cells, while APEX requires exogenous cofactors which may not be easily transported into worms (Branon et al., 2018; Rhee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Branon et al., 2018 and Rhee et al., 2013.

claim: TurboID catalyzes biotinylation with much greater efficiency than BioID.
source: (3) TurboID catalyzes biotinylation with much greater efficiency than BioID (Branon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Branon et al., 2018.

claim: TurboID fusion proteins can be toxic.
source: First, TurboID fusion proteins can be toxic.
evidence: This is inferred from the sterility phenotypes observed.

claim: TurboID labeled cytoplasmic proteins as revealed by streptavidin staining.
source: Second, TurboID labeled cytoplasmic proteins as revealed by streptavidin staining (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by streptavidin staining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Some proteins may be biotinylated by TurboID when passing through P granules and shuttling between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: It is possible that some proteins are biotinylated by TurboID when passing through P granules and shuttling between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the labeling of cytoplasmic proteins.

claim: Because P granules are membraneless and highly dynamic, the bait proteins (GLH-1 and DEPS-1) may constantly mix and de-mix with surrounding cytoplasmic components.
source: Alternatively, because P granules are membraneless and highly dynamic, the bait proteins (GLH-1 and DEPS-1) may constantly mix and de-mix with surrounding cytoplasmic components.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the labeling of cytoplasmic proteins.

claim: An auxin-inducible degradation system can be applied to deplete the toxic TurboID fusion proteins.
source: For example, an auxin-inducible degradation system can be applied to deplete the toxic TurboID fusion proteins (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments based on citation.

claim: A split-TurboID method was developed, in which TurboID is split into two inactive fragments, but can be reconstituted in vivo.
source: More recently, a split-TurboID method was developed, in which TurboID is split into two inactive fragments, but can be reconstituted in vivo (Cho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cho et al., 2020.

claim: Fusing individual fragments of TurboID into two P granule proteins will improve the specificity in labeling P granule proteins.
source: We envision this approach will greatly improve the specificity in labeling P granule proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future applications.

claim: C. elegans germ cells possess other membraneless organelles such as Z granules and Mutator foci.
source: In addition to P granules, C. elegans germ cells possess other membraneless organelles such as Z granules and Mutator foci (Phillips et al., 2012; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2012 and Wan et al., 2018.

claim: Z granules and Mutator foci are adjacent to P granules, but each has distinct functions in RNAi and transgenerational epigenetic inheritance.
source: These granules are adjacent to one another, but each has distinct functions in RNAi and transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (Phillips et al., 2012; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2012 and Wan et al., 2018.

claim: P granules, Z granules, and Mutator foci share some common proteins, but also contain unique components.
source: We speculate that they share some common proteins, but also contain unique components.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the distinct functions of these granules.

claim: Proximity labeling can be applied to unravel the proteome of Z granules and Mutator foci.
source: Proximity labeling described in this study can be applied to unravel the proteome of Z granules and Mutator foci, and thus will provide new insight into the organization and function of germ granules.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future applications of the method.
